definition: One of two or more nuclides of the same element: they have the same proton number $Z$ but different numbers of neutrons, so different nucleon numbers $A$.
The total mass of the separate protons and neutrons that make up a nucleus minus the mass of the nucleus itself, $\Delta m$; the nucleus always has the smaller mass.

The minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus completely into its individual nucleons, equal to the energy released when the nucleus forms from them: $E_\text{B} = \Delta m\, c^{2}$, where $\Delta m$ is the mass defect.
The binding energy of a nucleus divided by its nucleon number; the higher it is, the more tightly bound the nucleus, with a peak of about 8.8 MeV near iron-56.

The principle that mass and energy are equivalent, $E = mc^{2}$: when a system's energy changes by $\Delta E$, its mass changes by $\Delta E / c^{2}$, so a nuclear reaction that releases energy ends with less mass.
The attractive force between nucleons that holds a nucleus together; it acts only over distances of about $10^{-15}\ \text{m}$, where it is stronger than the electric repulsion between protons.
